Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 63, verses 1–3:

Medinan, and it is eleven verses [revealed after the Hajj]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

By their saying "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah" they meant a testimony in which their hearts agreed with their tongues. [Mahmud said: "It is only that He called them liars because they claimed that their testimony with their tongues agreed with their hearts... etc." Ahmad said: Like this, from his elegant manner, is His saying: "The Bedouins say, 'We have believed.' Say: 'You have not believed, but say, "We have submitted."'" The sentence that would correspond to His saying "but say, we have submitted" would have been to say to them, "Do not say, we have believed." But since it would give the impression of forbidding the saying of faith, He turned away from it, despite the antithesis it contains, to what leaves the statement free of that misunderstanding. That is more important and greater than the benefit of antithesis, especially when addressing those who followed what is ambiguous in it, seeking discord. Do you not see how they deceived themselves, feigning ignorance, and disguised their weakness, pretending not to understand, when there was revealed His saying: "Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell"?]. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said: They said that, and Allah knows that the matter is as their saying indicates, that you are the Messenger of Allah, and Allah bears witness that they are liars in their saying "We bear witness," and in their claim of agreement in it. Or: they are liars in it, because if it is devoid of agreement of heart it is not truly a testimony, so they are lying in calling it a testimony. Or he meant: Allah bears witness that they are liars in their own estimation, because they believed that their saying "You are indeed the Messenger of Allah" was a falsehood and a report contrary to the actual state of what was reported. If you say: What is the benefit of His saying, "And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger"?

I say: If He had said, "They say, 'We bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah,' and Allah bears witness that they are the liars," it would have implied that their saying was false, so He inserted between them His saying "And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger" to remove this implication. "They have taken their oaths as a shield" may mean that their saying "We bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah" is one of their false oaths, because testimony takes the place of swearing in what is meant by emphasis. A man says, "I bear witness and I bear witness by Allah," "I resolve and I resolve by Allah," in place of "I swear" and "I swear by Allah." By this Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, cited evidence that "I bear witness" is an oath. [Mahmud said: "He argued for Abu Hanifa that the saying of one who says 'I bear witness' is an oath, from His saying 'They have taken their oaths as a shield,' though nothing came from them except their saying 'We bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah,' so He made it an oath." Ahmad said: One of the two opinions of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is that if one says "I bear witness," "I swear," or "I take an oath" without intending by Allah or anything else, it is an oath; this is not the well-known view. As for if he intends by Allah, even without pronouncing it, it is clearly an oath without difficulty. There is no evidence in what he mentioned for what he stated, for His saying "They have taken their oaths as a shield" only means that what they said is called an oath, and the disagreement is not about naming it an oath; the disagreement is whether it becomes a binding oath whose violation requires expiation or not.

Not everything called an oath or a swearing creates a legal ruling. Do you not see that if he says, "I swear," without saying "by Allah" or anything else, it is among the matters of disagreement regarding whether expiation is due for it, even though it is an oath linguistically by agreement, because it is a derivative verb from it.]. It may also be a description of the hypocrites in their concealment behind oaths. Al-Hasan al-Basri read "īmānahum" (their faith), meaning what they displayed of faith with their tongues. His saying, "That is because they believed, then disbelieved," supports this. "Evil is what they used to do": from their hypocrisy and their obstruction of people from the way of Allah. In "evil is" there is a sense of wonder, which is an exaltation of their matter in the hearers' minds. "That" refers to His saying "Evil is what they used to do," i.e., that saying which bears witness against them that they are the worst of people in their deeds, because of "that they believed, then disbelieved," or it refers to what was described of their condition in hypocrisy, lying, and concealing themselves behind oaths; that is, all of that is because they believed, then disbelieved, "so a seal was set upon their hearts," so they became bold toward every grave matter. If you say: The hypocrites were only upon constant, established disbelief... [Mahmud said: "The hypocrites were only upon constant, established disbelief... etc." Ahmad said: It may also bear a fourth aspect: that they believed in him before his mission, according to the description in the Torah, for they used to hear it from their Jewish neighbours; then they disbelieved in him after his mission and the matching of the description. Perhaps among the hypocrites there were Jews, and if not, faith before his mission existed among both groups: the Jews and the idolaters of the Arabs, until the revelation of His saying: "Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the idolaters were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence." How Allah related what each of the two groups used to say. "Clear evidence" means the Prophet ﷺ.] Then what is the meaning of His saying, "they believed, then disbelieved"? I say: There are three aspects. The first: "they believed" means they uttered the words of testimony and acted as one who enters Islam does; then "they disbelieved" means their disbelief later became apparent and was made clear by what was known of their statements, such as their saying: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are donkeys," and their saying during the expedition of Tabuk: "Does this man hope that the palaces of Kisra and Caesar will be opened to him? Far-fetched!" Similar is His saying: "They swear by Allah that they did not say it, but they did say the word of disbelief and disbelieved after their submission." That is: their disbelief became apparent after they had embraced Islam. Similar is His saying: "Make no excuses; you have disbelieved after your faith." The second: "they believed" means they uttered faith in the presence of the believers, then they uttered disbelief in the presence of their devils, mocking Islam, as in His saying: "When they meet those who believe, they say, 'We believe'... until His saying, 'We are only mockers.'" The third: that the reference is to the apostates among them.

It is also recited: "fa-tubi'a 'ala qulubihim" (so a seal was set upon their hearts, in the passive). Zayd ibn Ali recited: "fa-taba'a Allahu" (so Allah set a seal).

Abdullah ibn Ubayy was a man of large build and handsome appearance, eloquent, sharp of tongue [[His words "eloquent, sharp of tongue" mean fluent of tongue, as stated in the Sihah. (A)]], and a group of the hypocrites shared his description; they were the leaders of Madinah. They used to attend the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and lean back in it, and they had imposing looks and eloquent tongues. [[Mahmud said: "They used to sit with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and lean back in the assembly, and they had imposing looks and eloquent tongues..." etc. Ahmad said: There is a point of concern in what al-Yazidi said from the standpoint of Arabic grammar; otherwise the meaning is sound. The word is recited with a damma and with a sukun on the shin, both being widely transmitted readings. This is evidence that its original form is with damma, and the sukun is a later development for lightening. This makes it unlikely that it is the plural of khashbaa' on the pattern fa'lā', because the regular plural of that is fu'l with a sukun on the middle letter, like hamra' and hamr, and a damma does not arise. Had it been as he said, its shin would not have been vowelled with damma. And Allah knows best.]] So the Prophet (ﷺ) and those present were impressed by their physical forms and listened to their speech. If you ask: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿as if they were propped-up timber﴾? I say:

They are likened, in their leaning, while they are nothing but empty bodies void of faith and good, to timber propped against a wall. Timber, when it is put to use, is in roofs, walls, or other places of benefit; and as long as it is left idle and unused, it is propped against a wall, so they were likened to it in being of no benefit. It is also permissible that by "propped-up timber" is meant idols carved from wood and propped against walls, and they were likened to these in the beauty of their forms and the scarcity of their usefulness. The address in ﴿you see them, their bodies please you﴾ is to the Messenger of Allah, or to anyone who is addressed. It is also read as "yusma'" (is heard) in the passive voice. The position of ﴿as if they were propped-up timber﴾ is nominative: "they are as if they were propped-up timber," or it is a new sentence with no grammatical place. It is also read as "khushub," the plural of "khushbah," like "budnah" and "budn," and "khushub" like "thamarah" and "thamar," and "khushub" like "mudrah" and "mudr"; the last is in the reading of Ibn Abbas. It is also reported from al-Yazidi that he said regarding "khushub" that it is the plural of "khashbaa'", and the khashbaa' is the piece of timber whose inside has rotted [[His words "whose inside has rotted" mean decayed, according to the Sihah. (A)]]; they were likened to it in their hypocrisy and the corruption of their inner selves. ﴿They think every cry is against them﴾: ʿalayhim is the second object of yahsabun, meaning: they think every cry is directed against them and harmful to them, because of their cowardice, their panic, and the terror in their hearts:

When a caller calls out in the camp, or an animal escapes, or a lost thing is announced, they think it is an attack upon them. It is also said: they were in dread lest God send down upon them what would expose their secrets and make their blood and wealth lawful. From this al-Akhtal took his line: "You have never ceased to think every thing after them to be horsemen charging against them and men [[Al-Akhtal says: O Jarir, you still think everything after them, i.e., after the abandonment by your people, to be ... It is also permissible that "after them" means "other than them": horsemen charging, i.e., returning swiftly against them, and men, because of how much fear has settled in your heart.]]."

ʿalayhim is stopped upon, and ﴿they are the enemy﴾ is begun: that is, the ones complete in enmity, because the worst enemy is the deceiving enemy, the one who flatters you while the disease of resentment lies beneath his ribs. ﴿So beware of them﴾ and do not be deceived by their outward appearance.

It is also permissible that ﴿they are the enemy﴾ be the second object, as if you had dropped the pronoun. If you ask: then it should be said "she is the enemy"; I say: it is regarded in view of the predicate, as in His saying "this is my Lord." And it is possible to supply an omitted modifier: "they think every person of cry..." — ﴿May Allah fight them﴾: a supplication against them, and a request from Him that He curse them and disgrace them; or it is a teaching to the believers that they should invoke this against them. ﴿How are they turned away?﴾ — how do they turn aside from the truth, marvelling at their ignorance and misguidance [[His words "marvelling at their ignorance" perhaps mean "a marvel," or even "a cause of marvel." (A)]].

They turned their heads (لَوَّوْا رُؤُسَهُمْ): they twisted them aside and inclined them, turning away from that and in arrogance. It is also read with the light and the heavy forms (بالتخفيف والتشديد), the heavy form (لَوَّوْا) being for intensification.

They turned their heads (لَوَّوْا رُؤُسَهُمْ): they twisted them aside and inclined them, turning away from that and in arrogance. It is also read with the light and the heavy forms (بالتخفيف والتشديد), the heavy form (لَوَّوْا) being for intensification.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 63, verses 7–8:

It is narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met the Banu al-Mustaliq at al-Muraysi', which was their water-source, he defeated them and killed some of them. Jahjah ibn Sa'id, a hired man of Umar who was leading his horse, and Sinan al-Juhani, an ally of Abdullah ibn Ubayy, crowded around the water and fought with each other. Jahjah shouted, "O Muhajirun!" and Sinan shouted, "O Ansar!" Ju'al, one of the poor Muhajirun, came to Jahjah's aid and slapped Sinan. Abdullah said to Ju'al, "And you are there?" He also said, "We have accompanied Muhammad only so that we might be slapped! By Allah, our situation and theirs is only like the saying: 'Fatten your dog and it will devour you.' By Allah, if we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it." By "the mightier" he meant himself, and by "the meaner" he meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he said to his people, "What have you done to yourselves? You have settled them in your land and shared your wealth with them. By Allah, if you withheld food from Ju'al and his kin, they would not ride on your necks, and they would soon move away from you. So do not spend on them until they disperse from around Muhammad."

Zayd ibn Arqam, who was a youth, heard this and said, "By Allah, you are the lowly, the few, the hated among your people, while Muhammad is in the might of the Merciful and the strength of the Muslims." Abdullah said, "Be quiet, for I was only joking." Zayd informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Umar said, "Let me strike the neck of this hypocrite, O Messenger of Allah!" He said, "Then the noses of many would be made to tremble in Yathrib." Umar said, "If you dislike that my fellow Muhajir should kill him, then order an Ansari to do it." He said, "Then how would it be when people say that Muhammad kills his companions?"

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to Abdullah, "Are you the one whose words have reached me?" He said, "By Allah, who revealed the Book to you, I did not say anything of that sort, and Zayd is a liar." This is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾. Those present said, "O Messenger of Allah, our elder and our chief should not be believed over the words of a boy; perhaps he has made a mistake." It is also narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Zayd, "Perhaps you were angry with him?" He said, "No." He said, "Perhaps your hearing deceived you?" He said, "No." He said, "Perhaps it was confused for you?" He said, "No."

When the revelation came down, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) caught up with Zayd from behind, tugged his ear and said, "Your ear has been made true, O boy. Allah has confirmed you and has declared the hypocrites liars." [[Thus al-Waqidi mentioned it in his Maghazi without an isnad, and attributed it to al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and the authors of the biographies. Ibn Ishaq recorded it in his Sirah: "Asim ibn Umar ibn Qatadah, Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr and Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban each narrated to me part of the account of the Banu al-Mustaliq," and he mentioned the whole expedition and the aforementioned story with slight variation. Al-Tabari also recorded it through his route. The root of the story is in the two Sahihs, through the route of Abu Ishaq from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "I was with my uncle and I heard Abdullah ibn Ubayy say..." — the hadith — and its beginning is also in both of them through the route of Amr ibn Dinar from Jabir, who said: "We were on the expedition of the Banu al-Mustaliq when a man of the Muhajirun pursued a man of the Ansar." Al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and al-Hakim narrated it through the route of Abu Sa'd al-Awdi: "Zayd ibn Arqam said: We campaigned with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and there were some Bedouins with us, and we used to race to the water, but the Bedouins would outpace us, and a Bedouin got ahead and filled the basin," and he mentioned the story in full. There is variation in its wording.]]

When Abdullah wanted to enter Medina, his son Hubab confronted him. He was Abdullah ibn Abdullah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had changed his name. He said, "Hubab is the name of a devil." He was sincere, and he said, "Stay where you are! By Allah, you shall not enter it until you say that the Messenger of Allah is the mighty and you are the lowly." He kept him confined in his hand until the Messenger of Allah ordered that he be released. [[Thus al-Tha'labi mentioned it connected to the preceding account. It is narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met the Banu al-Mustaliq at al-Muraysi', which was their water-source, he defeated them and killed some of them. Jahjah ibn Sa'id, a hired man of Umar who was leading his horse, and Sinan al-Juhani, an ally of Abdullah ibn Ubayy, crowded around the water and fought with each other. Jahjah shouted, "O Muhajirun!" and Sinan shouted, "O Ansar!" Ju'al, one of the poor Muhajirun, came to Jahjah's aid and slapped Sinan. Abdullah said to Ju'al, "And you are there?" He also said, "We have accompanied Muhammad only so that we might be slapped! By Allah, our situation and theirs is only like the saying: 'Fatten your dog and it will devour you.' By Allah, if we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it." By "the mightier" he meant himself, and by "the meaner" he meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he said to his people, "What have you done to yourselves? You have settled them in your land and shared your wealth with them. By Allah, if you withheld food from Ju'al and his kin, they would not ride on your necks, and they would soon move away from you. So do not spend on them until they disperse from around Muhammad."

Zayd ibn Arqam, who was a youth, heard this and said, "By Allah, you are the lowly, the few, the hated among your people, while Muhammad is in the might of the Merciful and the strength of the Muslims." Abdullah said, "Be quiet, for I was only joking." Zayd informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Umar said, "Let me strike the neck of this hypocrite, O Messenger of Allah!" He said, "Then the noses of many would be made to tremble in Yathrib." Umar said, "If you dislike that my fellow Muhajir should kill him, then order an Ansari to do it." He said, "Then how would it be when people say that Muhammad kills his companions?"

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to Abdullah, "Are you the one whose words have reached me?" He said, "By Allah, who revealed the Book to you, I did not say anything of that sort, and Zayd is a liar." This is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾. Those present said, "O Messenger of Allah, our elder and our chief should not be believed over the words of a boy; perhaps he has made a mistake." It is also narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Zayd, "Perhaps you were angry with him?" He said, "No." He said, "Perhaps your hearing deceived you?" He said, "No." He said, "Perhaps it was confused for you?" He said, "No."

When the revelation came down, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) caught up with Zayd from behind, tugged his ear and said, "Your ear has been made true, O boy. Allah has confirmed you and has declared the hypocrites liars." [[Thus al-Waqidi mentioned it in his Maghazi without an isnad, and attributed it to al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and the authors of the biographies. Ibn Ishaq recorded it in his Sirah: "Asim ibn Umar ibn Qatadah, Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr and Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban each narrated to me part of the account of the Banu al-Mustaliq," and he mentioned the whole expedition and the aforementioned story with slight variation. There is variation in its wording.]]

Do not let your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of God. (Lit.: "Let not your wealth distract you," i.e., do not let your concern with managing and disposing of it, and your eagerness to seek its increase through trade and cultivation, its offspring and its enjoyment, and your delight in its benefits, distract you; "nor your children," i.e., your joy in them, your compassion for them, your attending to their needs, and arranging what will set them right in their livelihood both during your lifetime and after your death.) You know the measure of the benefit of wealth and children, and that it is the least and lowest of things compared with what is with God, "from the remembrance of God," i.e., preferring it over them. "And whoever does that," i.e., intends preoccupation with this world at the expense of religion, "those are the losers," in their trade, since they have exchanged the great and enduring for the paltry and perishing. And it has been said:

The remembrance of God means the five daily prayers. It is reported from al-Hasan: all the obligatory duties, as if he said: "from obedience to God." And it has been said:

The Qur'an. And it is reported from al-Kalbi: jihad alongside the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 63, verses 10–11:

"Min" in ﴿مِمَّا رَزَقْناكُمْ﴾ (from what We have provided for you) is partitive (lil-tab'id), and what is meant is obligatory spending, ﴿مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ يَأْتِيَ أَحَدَكُمُ الْمَوْتُ﴾ (before death comes to one of you), that is, before he sees the signs of death and witnesses what makes him despair of being given more time, when his throat is constricted, when spending becomes impossible for him, and when the time of acceptance has passed. Then he regrets his withholding and bites his fingertips (ya'addu anamilahu) over the loss of what he had been able to possess.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Give charity before the authority of death descends upon you, for then repentance will not be accepted and deeds will not benefit."

And from him: "What prevents one of you, when he has wealth, from paying zakat, and when he is able to perform Hajj, from performing it before death comes to him, so that he asks his Lord for a return and is not granted it?"

And from him: "It was revealed concerning those who withhold zakat. By Allah, if he had seen good, he would not have asked for a return." It was said to him: "Do you not fear Allah? The believers ask for a return?" He said: "Yes, I recite to you a Qur'an about it." That is, it was revealed concerning the believers, and they are the ones addressed by it.

Similarly, from al-Hasan: "No one who has not paid zakat, not fasted, and not performed Hajj fails to ask for a return."

And from 'Ikrimah: it was revealed concerning the people of the qibla (Muslims): ﴿لَوْلا أَخَّرْتَنِي﴾ (why did You not delay me).

It has been recited as "akhkhartan" (أخرتن), meaning: "Why did You not postpone my death to a near term, a little time," ﴿فَأَصَّدَّقَ﴾ (so that I may give charity). Ubayy recited "fa-atasaddaqa" (فأتصدق) according to the original form. It has also been recited "wa-akun" (وأكن), as a conjunction with the place (mahall) of ﴿فَأَصَّدَّقَ﴾, as if it were said: "If You delay me, I shall give charity and be among the righteous." Whoever recites "wa-akuna" (وأكون) in the accusative takes it according to the wording (lafz). 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr recited "wa-akūnu" (وأكون), meaning "and I would be," a promise of righteousness from him.

﴿وَلَنْ يُؤَخِّرَ اللَّهُ﴾ (but Allah will never delay) is a negation of delay, in an emphatic form whose meaning is that the negated thing contradicts wisdom. The meaning is: when you know that delaying death beyond its appointed time is something there is no way to, and that it will surely come upon you suddenly, and that Allah is aware of your deeds and will requite them, whether withholding what is obligatory or otherwise, then nothing remains but to hasten to discharge the obligations and prepare to meet Allah.

It has been recited "ta'malūna" (تعملون) with ta' and ya' (both readings).

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Munafiqun will be free from hypocrisy." [Narrated by Ibn Mardawayh, al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi with their chains going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]
